metadata.title: Education systems and social background inequality of educational opportunity: New evidence

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 with the standard two-stage sampling design (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then students sampled within schools). The dependent variable is constructed from PISA plausible values (10 PVs per domain) using weighted averages, and the overall achievement score is a weighted average across mathematics, reading, and science. The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling weights (and any replicate weights) were explicitly applied in the fixed-effects regressions; therefore, weight usage cannot be confirmed from the text. The analysis clusters standard errors at the school level to address within-school non-independence, but this is not the same as applying complex-survey weights.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper uses PISA plausible values and constructs domain scores as weighted averages of the 10 PVs, but it does not describe any explicit missing-data strategy for background variables (e.g., ESCS, immigration status, language at home) or for controls. Because the study relies on regression models with a large analytic sample, missingness handling is likely handled implicitly by PISA item nonresponse procedures and/or listwise deletion, but the authors do not document which approach was used. This omission limits reproducibility and makes it unclear whether missingness could bias the estimated interactions.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA microdata from the 2015 and 2018 cycles for 15-year-old students. It excludes PISA 2022 due to COVID-19-related low response rates in 13 participating countries and potential comparability issues. The analytic sample is restricted to students with available PISA ESCS (family background) and the specified control variables (gender, age, grade, immigration status, home language categories) used in the fixed-effects regressions; however, the manuscript does not specify the exact missing-data rule (e.g., complete cases vs. imputation). No additional grade or school-type restrictions are described beyond the standard PISA eligibility and sampling.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Country fixed-effects regression (clustered SE at school level). Model 1: Family background=21.218*** (0.466); Family background × SGUSE=6.832*** (0.701). Model 2: Family background=18.282*** (0.511); Family background × SGUSE=4.108*** (0.752); Family background × HST=9.188*** (0.762). R²: 0.469 (Model 1), 0.470 (Model 2). Sample size: 181,727.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 and 2018 the study leveraged family background (ESCS) together with SGUSE stratification and HST transition exams (plus demographic controls) to model academic achievement, finding that the family background–achievement association is stronger in highly stratified general upper secondary education systems and is further strengthened when HST is present. This indicates that education-system design—especially stratification within general upper secondary schooling and selective/standardized lower-to-upper transition examinations—may amplify social-background inequality of educational opportunity, suggesting that policy reforms should target these institutional mechanisms to reduce equity gaps.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 and PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students across 49 countries to examine how education-system features moderate the relationship between family background (ESCS) and academic achievement. Achievement is constructed from PISA plausible values by taking weighted averages across the 10 PVs for mathematics, reading, and science, then averaging across domains into an overall score. The analysis applies a country fixed-effects model with clustered standard errors at the school level, estimating interactions between ESCS and two system indicators: SGUSE (high vs. low stratification) and HST (presence of standardized, selective lower-to-upper transition exams). Results show that ESCS has a positive association with achievement and that ESCS×SGUSE and ESCS×HST interactions are statistically significant (Model 1: ESCS×SGUSE=6.832***; Model 2: ESCS×SGUSE=4.108*** and ESCS×HST=9.188***; R²≈0.47; N=181,727). Limitations include the lack of an explicit missing-data strategy and the fact that the approach is not ML predictive modeling (no ML algorithms, weights, or PV-combining method beyond PV averaging are reported).
